raw_text:
# Transcaval Access for Large-Bore Structural Heart and Endovascular Interventions: A Narrative Review

Large-bore transcatheter interventions, particularly transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and temporary percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (MCS), have revolutionized structural cardiology. Although retrograde transfemoral access is the gold-standard route, severe peripheral artery disease, arterial tortuosity, and heavy calcification frequently render it prohibitive. Traditional surgical alternatives, such as transapical and transaortic access, are associated with significant patient morbidity. To overcome these limitations, a novel percutaneous, extra-thoracic alternative—transcaval (caval-aortic) access—was developed.

### Preclinical and Early Clinical Evolution
The concept of transcaval access was first validated in pre-clinical porcine models by Halabi and colleagues, demonstrating that high-caliber sheath passage from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent abdominal aorta was anatomically feasible [1]. This was quickly translated into the clinical arena, with the first-in-human experience published in 2014 by Greenbaum et al., establishing safety and feasibility in high-risk patients who lacked other access options [2].

A defining feature of the transcaval approach is its absolute reliance on advanced imaging. An early imaging study by Chen and colleagues demonstrated that precise pre-procedural planning using multidetector computed tomography (CT) is mandatory to identify a calcium-free target window on the abdominal aorta directly adjacent to the IVC, while avoiding major arterial branches or overlying bowel structures [3]. The versatility of this access was further extended to complex anatomies, including patients with previously implanted synthetic polyester abdominal aortic grafts [4]. To assist clinical dissemination, Lederman et al. published a comprehensive step-by-step technical guide for vascular crossing and closure [5]. This path was also adapted to treat thoracic aortic pathologies, with Uflacker et al. reporting the initial human experience of transcaval access for thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [6]. Furthermore, the introduction of expandable sheath technology enabled low-profile entry with high-caliber internal expansion, reducing vascular trauma [7].

### Contemporary Procedural Technique and Best Practices
As the technique matured, a milestone prospectively adjudicated clinical trial of 100 patients (the NHLBI Transcaval TAVR Study) established its safety profile, with a 99% access success rate and 98% closure success [8]. Standardizing patient selection, Lederman et al. outlined formal CT-based anatomical suitability criteria [9]. Electrosurgical crossing is the gold-standard traversal method; however, for highly calcified or resistant vessel walls, laser-assisted crossing has also been successfully described [10].

The clinical safety of transcaval access derives from a unique pressure gradient: the surrounding retroperitoneal interstitial space pressure exceeds venous pressure, causing any blood exiting the abdominal aortotomy to decompress harmlessly into the lower-pressure IVC [8]. This forms a temporary, hemodynamically benign aortocaval fistula [8]. Core-laboratory CT follow-up at 12 months showed that 93% of these fistulas closed spontaneously after deploying nitinol cardiac occluders off-label [11]. To simplify this process and avoid off-label device utilization, dedicated transcaval closure systems have undergone clinical trials [12].

In the clinical setting, transcaval access has expanded beyond simple anatomy. It has been used to deliver biventricular mechanical support using complete venous access [13]. A multicentre European registry further confirmed the reproducibility of transcaval access across diverse clinical sites [14]. Comparative cohorts have shown that transcaval access offers similar or superior 30-day outcomes when compared to other non-femoral routes, such as subclavian or transaxillary access [15,16].

### Wider Applications, Complications, and Closure
Beyond routine TAVR, transcaval access is vital in the management of cardiogenic shock, facilitating the emergency delivery of high-flow MCS devices like the Impella 5.0 without the risk of limb ischemia [17]. A large multicenter propensity-weighted analysis demonstrated that transcaval TAVR is associated with a five-fold lower risk of stroke compared to transaxillary TAVR, with similar bleeding rates and more frequent direct-to-home discharges [18]. It has also been evaluated as a feasible alternative in morbidly obese patients who frequently suffer from high-risk femoral access complications [19].

To guide clinical practice, a state-of-the-art review compiled best practices for procedural troubleshooting [20]. Recent large-scale systematic reviews and meta-analyses have consolidated these findings, showing that transcaval access achieves a ~95% procedural success rate with short-term mortality and complication rates similar to supra-aortic approaches [21,22].

In vascular surgery, transcaval access is widely utilized for embolizing persistent type II endoleaks after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) [23,24,25]. Clinical registries have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of percutaneous mechanical circulatory support delivered via transcaval access [26]. Furthermore, step-by-step guidance has been published for performing transcaval TAVR in patients with bicuspid aortic valves [27]. A systematic review highlighted that the transcaval approach remains a highly versatile pathway for various endovascular aortic interventions [28]. This clinical utility is further supported by JACC state-of-the-art electrosurgery reviews [29] and the "7 pillars" framework for managing transcaval TAVR [30].
